questions.q: Name one physical, one emotional and one social change of adolescence.
questions.a: Physical: growth spurt; emotional: mood swings; social: more time with friends/independence.

days.guide: Review boundaries and communication with quick role-plays.

questions.q: Give an assertive boundary statement.
questions.a: 'I don't want to talk about that. Please stop.'

days.guide: Your child checks progress on sleep and hygiene goals and adjusts.

questions.q: If you averaged 7.5 hours and your goal was 9, what change could help?
questions.a: Move bedtime earlier by 30–60 minutes, set a screen curfew, keep a consistent wake time.

days.guide: Give the unit 5 test (see key).

questions.q: What is the endocrine system?
questions.a: Glands that release hormones into the blood to control growth, metabolism and development.

days.guide: Talk with your child about what they learned and any lingering questions.

questions.q: What's one thing you learned that you'll use?
questions.a: Open answer — look for a specific skill such as a sleep routine or boundary statement.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test (suggested): 1) puberty is caused by hormones 2) timing varies (about ages 8–14 start) 3) teens need 8–10 hours of sleep 4) screens/blue light reduce melatonin 5) acne caused by oil, clogged pores, bacteria, hormones 6) brush twice, floss once daily 7) pituitary = master gland 8) three boundary types (physical, emotional, digital) 9) consent = freely given, can be withdrawn 10) two valid resources. 9–10 advanced, 7–8 proficient.

weeks.prep: Glitter or Glo Germ lotion, soap, paper towels. Print a simple immune-system diagram. Read CDC 'How vaccines work.'
misconceptions: Taking antibiotics for a cold or flu. Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses; misuse causes antibiotic resistance.
Thinking hand sanitizer is always as good as soap. Soap and water for 20 seconds is best, especially when hands are visibly dirty.

days.guide: Your child compares the four pathogen types in a chart with an example disease each.

questions.q: What is the difference between bacteria and viruses?
questions.a: Bacteria are living single cells that can reproduce on their own; viruses are much smaller and must invade a host cell to reproduce.

questions.q: Name a disease caused by a fungus.
questions.a: Athlete's foot, ringworm or a yeast infection.

days.guide: Put glitter on your child's hand, shake hands, touch items, then see the spread. Wash with water only vs soap for 20 seconds and compare.

questions.q: Which removed more glitter — water alone or soap and scrubbing 20 seconds?
questions.a: Soap and scrubbing for 20 seconds.

questions.q: Name three ways germs spread.
questions.a: Direct contact, coughs/sneezes (droplets), contaminated surfaces, food or water, insect bites.

days.guide: Diagram: skin/mucus barriers → inflammation/fever → white blood cells → antibodies and memory cells.

questions.q: What are antibodies?
questions.a: Proteins made by white blood cells that recognize and help destroy specific pathogens.

questions.q: What is the body's first line of defense?
questions.a: Skin and mucous membranes (plus tears, saliva, stomach acid).

days.guide: Explain how vaccines create immune memory without the illness, and herd immunity.

questions.q: How does a vaccine work?
questions.a: It exposes the immune system to a harmless form or part of a germ so it makes antibodies and memory cells, ready to fight the real germ quickly.

questions.q: Who does herd immunity protect?
questions.a: People who can't be vaccinated, such as newborns or people with weak immune systems.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key.

questions.q: Will antibiotics cure the flu?
questions.a: No — the flu is caused by a virus; antibiotics only work against bacteria.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (suggested): 1) pathogen = germ that causes disease 2) bacteria = single-celled living organisms (strep throat), some treated with antibiotics 3) viruses = must invade cells to reproduce (cold, flu, COVID-19); not killed by antibiotics 4) fungi = athlete's foot, ringworm 5) parasites = lice, giardia, tapeworms 6) spread: direct contact, droplets/air, contaminated food/water, vectors (mosquitoes, ticks), contaminated surfaces 7) white blood cells and antibodies fight infection 8) vaccines train the immune system using a harmless piece or weakened/inactivated form of a germ 9) herd immunity = when enough people are immune, spread is limited, protecting those who can't be vaccinated 10) wash 20 seconds.

weeks.prep: Find CDC or American Heart/Diabetes Association pages on heart disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer and asthma. Print a family health history form (e.g., CDC 'My Family Health Portrait'). Talk with relatives about health history in advance.
misconceptions: Thinking chronic diseases only affect old people. Habits formed now (diet, activity, not smoking) affect risk later, and type 2 diabetes and asthma occur in teens.
Believing a family history means you will definitely get the disease. It raises risk, but healthy behaviors can lower it.

days.guide: Your child researches four chronic diseases: cause, symptoms, risk factors.

questions.q: What happens in type 2 diabetes?
questions.a: The body doesn't use insulin well (insulin resistance), so blood sugar stays too high.

questions.q: What is asthma?
questions.a: A chronic disease where airways become inflamed and narrow, causing wheezing, coughing and shortness of breath; triggers include smoke, pollen, exercise and cold air.

days.guide: Sort risk factors: uncontrollable (age, genes, family history, sex) vs controllable (diet, activity, smoking, sleep, sun exposure).

questions.q: Is family history a controllable risk factor?
questions.a: No — it is uncontrollable.

questions.q: Name three controllable risk factors for heart disease.
questions.a: Smoking, inactivity, unhealthy diet high in saturated fat and sodium, high blood pressure, excess weight.

days.guide: Complete the family health history with a parent.

questions.q: Why does a doctor want your family health history?
questions.a: It shows which diseases you may be at higher risk for so you can screen earlier and prevent them.

days.guide: Connect MyPlate and 60 minutes of activity to lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.

questions.q: How does physical activity lower diabetes risk?
questions.a: Muscles use glucose, helping control blood sugar and improving insulin sensitivity; it also helps maintain a healthy weight.

days.guide: Your child writes a prevention plan; score with the rubric.

questions.q: Name one way to lower skin cancer risk.
questions.a: Use SPF 30+ sunscreen, wear hats/protective clothing, avoid tanning beds, seek shade midday.

weeks.assessment_key: Prevention plan rubric: 4 = names the disease and accurate description, lists 2 uncontrollable and 3 controllable risk factors, gives 3+ specific SMART prevention behaviors (e.g., 60 min activity daily, limit sugary drinks, never smoke, sunscreen), mentions screenings/checkups; 3 = most elements; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather your child's immunization record and recent checkup info. Prepare a list of local clinics, pharmacies, public health department. Personal health record template (name, allergies, medications, vaccinations, doctor/dentist contacts, insurance).
misconceptions: Thinking you only need a doctor when sick. Yearly well checkups and twice-yearly dental cleanings catch problems early.
Being afraid to ask doctors questions. Doctors expect questions; it's your body and your right to understand.

days.guide: Describe what happens at well checkups (height/weight, BP, vaccines, questions), dental (cleaning, X-rays, exam) and vision exams.

questions.q: How often should teens see a dentist?
questions.a: Usually every 6 months.

questions.q: Name two things a doctor checks at a well visit.
questions.a: Height and weight, blood pressure, vision/hearing, vaccines, heart and lungs, development, mental health.

days.guide: Explain screenings: scoliosis (spine curvature, bending forward test), vision (eye chart), hearing (beeps at different pitches).

questions.q: What is scoliosis?
questions.a: A sideways curve of the spine, often checked during growth spurts by having the person bend forward.

questions.q: Why screen people who feel fine?
questions.a: Screening finds problems early, before symptoms, when they're easier to treat.

days.guide: Map local health services on paper or online.

questions.q: What can a pharmacist help you with?
questions.a: Explaining how to take medicines, side effects, interactions, choosing OTC products, some vaccines.

days.guide: Role-play a doctor visit; your child prepares 3 questions and practices describing symptoms (when, where, how bad).

questions.q: Give one good question to ask your doctor.
questions.a: 'What does this medicine do, and what side effects should I watch for?' or 'Is my growth normal?'

days.guide: Your child completes the personal health record.

questions.q: Why keep a record of allergies and medications?
questions.a: So any doctor or emergency responder can treat you safely.

weeks.assessment_key: Personal health record: includes full name, birth date, emergency contacts, doctor/dentist names and phones, allergies, current medications, immunization dates, chronic conditions, and blood type if known. Proficient: complete and accurate, stored safely.

weeks.prep: Bookmark AirNow.gov. Find your water provider's annual Consumer Confidence (water quality) Report. Optional water test strips. A bag for a 1-day waste audit.
misconceptions: Thinking clear water is always safe. Lead and bacteria can't be seen; water reports and testing show safety.
Thinking sunscreen is only needed at the beach. UV rays reach you on cloudy days and during everyday outdoor activities.

days.guide: Check AirNow daily for a week; your child records AQI and the recommended action.

questions.q: What does an orange AQI day mean and who should act?
questions.a: Unhealthy for sensitive groups (101–150); people with asthma or heart/lung disease, children and older adults should reduce long or intense outdoor exercise.

questions.q: Name a source of air pollution.
questions.a: Vehicle exhaust, wildfire smoke, factories, power plants.

days.guide: Read the local water report: source (river, groundwater, imported) and any contaminants listed.

questions.q: Why is lead in water dangerous?
questions.a: Lead damages the brain and nervous system, especially in children, and has no safe level.

questions.q: Where does lead in water usually come from?
questions.a: Old lead pipes, solder or fixtures in plumbing.

days.guide: Teach noise-induced hearing loss (85 dB+, the 60/60 rule for earbuds: 60% volume, 60 minutes) and sun protection.

questions.q: What is the 60/60 rule for headphones?
questions.a: Listen at no more than 60% volume for no more than 60 minutes at a time.

questions.q: How often should sunscreen be reapplied?
questions.a: Every 2 hours, and after swimming or sweating.

days.guide: Audit one day's household trash; sort into landfill, recycling, compost; plan 3 reductions.

questions.q: Why is 'reduce' better than 'recycle'?
questions.a: Reducing prevents waste from being made at all, saving the energy and materials recycling still uses.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key.

questions.q: What does AQI stand for?
questions.a: Air Quality Index.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (suggested): 1) AQI colors: green good (0–50), yellow moderate (51–100), orange unhealthy for sensitive groups (101–150), red unhealthy (151–200), purple very unhealthy (201–300), maroon hazardous (301+) 2) on red days limit outdoor exercise 3) lead harms the brain and development, especially in children; found in old pipes and old paint 4) noise above about 85 dB over long periods damages hearing 5) sunscreen SPF 30+, reapply every 2 hours and after swimming 6) reduce, reuse, recycle in order of best impact.

weeks.prep: Help your child brainstorm local issues (vaping near parks, lack of bike lanes, air quality, water bottle refill stations, food access). Look up who makes decisions (city council, school board). Poster paper or slides.
misconceptions: Thinking one young person can't make a difference. Councils and boards respond to clear, polite, fact-based requests, and youth voices stand out.
Writing an advocacy piece with only opinions. Strong advocacy uses accurate facts, a personal connection and a specific request.

days.guide: Your child chooses an issue and gathers 3 facts from valid sources (cite them).

questions.q: Name two valid sources for community health data.
questions.a: County public health department, CDC, state health department, EPA/AirNow.

days.guide: Choose the format and audience; outline the message: issue, facts, personal connection, specific request.

questions.q: What is a stakeholder?
questions.a: A person or group affected by or able to influence the issue, such as residents, council members, parents, businesses.

days.guide: Create the product. Check facts and tone.

questions.q: Why should an advocacy letter be polite and specific?
questions.a: Decision-makers are more likely to listen and act on a respectful, concrete request.

days.guide: Present to family or send the letter/email to the decision-maker.

questions.q: What is your call to action?
questions.a: A specific request, e.g., 'Please install a water refill station at Central Park by next summer.'

days.guide: Your child reflects on what went well and possible impact.

questions.q: How could you measure whether your advocacy worked?
questions.a: Track replies, changes made, people who signed on or changed behavior.

weeks.assessment_key: Advocacy project rubric: 4 = clear health issue with 3+ facts from valid sources, identifies the audience/decision-maker, takes a clear stand, includes a specific, realistic request (call to action), polished and respectful; 3 = clear stand with 2 facts and a request; 2 = opinion with weak evidence; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Pull out the week 1 wellness wheel and the journal. Prepare a review game (Jeopardy categories: Nutrition, Mental Health, Safety, Drugs, Growth, Community Health) and a year-end exam.
misconceptions: Treating the wellness plan as a one-time document. Schedule check-ins to adjust.
Writing a plan without measurable goals. Each section needs a SMART goal.

days.guide: Your child redoes the wellness wheel and compares with week 1.

questions.q: Which area improved most and why?
questions.a: Open answer — look for a specific behavior change linked to a course skill.

days.guide: Play the review game across all six units.

questions.q: Name one skill from each of two units you'll keep using.
questions.a: Examples: reading labels (nutrition), box breathing (stress), refusal steps (drugs).

days.guide: Give the year-end exam (see key).

questions.q: What do clean, separate, cook and chill prevent?
questions.a: Foodborne illness.

days.guide: Your child writes a summer wellness plan with a SMART goal for each area.

questions.q: Write a SMART activity goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will bike or swim 45 minutes at least 5 days a week through August.'

days.guide: Share the plan with family and put check-in dates on the calendar.

questions.q: Why set check-in dates?
questions.a: They help you track progress, stay motivated and adjust the plan.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam (suggested 20 items, 2 from each area): six nutrients; 4 g sugar = 1 tsp; 60 min activity; clean-separate-cook-chill; stress signs and two coping strategies; 988; I-message formula; four bullying types; Drop-Cover-Hold On; 911 info; choking sign/abdominal thrusts; dopamine/prefrontal cortex; nicotine addiction; fentanyl and naloxone; refusal steps; puberty hormones; 8–10 hours sleep; consent; bacteria vs virus; vaccines/herd immunity; AQI. 18–20 advanced, 14–17 proficient. Wellness plan: SMART goals for nutrition, activity, sleep and stress, plus check-in dates.
